title: Present perfect simple and continuous
tagline: A finished result you can see now, or an activity that has been running up to this moment.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Speaking Part 2 — describing experience and change over time
why: The present perfect links the past to now, and B2 First tests both halves of it: the choice between simple (a result, a number, a first time) and continuous (an ongoing activity, its duration), plus the classic trap of for versus since. Get the time reference wrong and the whole sentence sounds like a translation.

marks.label: She is still swimming, and the period isn't over.

rows.label: Focus
cells: the activity — how long it went on

rows.label: Typical words
cells: already, yet, just, ever, how many

diagrams.title: for or since?
diagrams.caption: Both describe unfinished time — for counts the duration, since names the starting point.

head: Use
Form
Example
rows: I've lived in Lima for ten years.
Nadia has just finished her essay.
We haven't booked the tickets yet.
They've been rehearsing for two hours.
It's the best film I've ever seen.

use.point: Unfinished time: how long something has continued

examples.text: Mateo has played the guitar since he was eight.
We have known each other for almost three years now.
Miss Vega has taught at this school since 2018.

use.point: A finished result versus an ongoing activity

examples.text: Nadia has written two chapters of her story.
Nadia has been writing all weekend — her hand actually hurts.
examples.note: continuous — the activity itself, with visible evidence

examples.text: Look at the state of the kitchen — someone has been cooking.
examples.note: continuous — recent activity, evidence in the present

examples.text: Liam has just heard that the trip is confirmed.
Sofia has already finished the reading, so she's helping the others.

examples.note: yet = negative/question, not done at the time of speaking

examples.text: It's the most difficult exam we have ever taken.
This is the first time Liam has cooked for the whole team.

watch_out.wrong: I live here since five years.
watch_out.right: I've lived here for five years.
watch_out.why: For introduces a duration, not since, and unfinished time takes the present perfect, not the present simple.
A finished time word (yesterday) needs the past simple, never the present perfect.

watch_out.wrong: How long are you studying English?
watch_out.right: How long have you been studying English?
watch_out.why: How long with an unfinished action asks for the present perfect continuous.

watch_out.wrong: She has been finishing three exercises.
watch_out.why: A specific number or result takes the present perfect simple, not the continuous.

watch_out.wrong: I have never went to Cusco.
watch_out.why: The past participle of go is been or gone, not went.

watch_out.wrong: I know her since we were children.
watch_out.right: I've known her since we were children.
watch_out.why: A state verb in an unfinished-time sentence still needs the present perfect, not the present simple.

dialogue.title: Packing for Cusco
dialogue.context: Mateo and Nadia are checking what still needs doing before the school trip, while Miss Vega looks over the list.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Right, have you two finished the packing list yet?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Almost. I've been checking it all morning — we're just missing the medical forms.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I've already sent mine. Nadia, have you emailed yours to the office?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Not yet — my mum hasn't signed it. She's been so busy this week.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: How long have you been waiting for her to sign it?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Since Monday. I'll ask her tonight, I promise.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: This is the first proper trip we've had since Year 8, right?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Exactly — and it's been years since a group has been this organised.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: We've worked hard on it! Sofia and Liam have made the whole itinerary.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good. Get that form signed and we're all set.

items.sentence: Sofia ___ three letters this evening, and she's about to write a fourth.
items.why: a countable result (three letters) → present perfect simple

items.sentence: Miss Vega ___ at this school since 2018.
items.why: since + a point in time → present perfect
visible present evidence of a recent activity → present perfect continuous

items.sentence: I ___ him since we were at primary school together.
items.why: a state verb in unfinished time → present perfect

items.sentence: We ___ to Arequipa last summer, not this year.
items.why: a finished time word (last summer) → past simple

items.sentence: This is the best pizza I ___.
items.why: superlative + present perfect for an experience up to now

items.sentence: Liam ___ his homework yet, so he can't come out.
items.why: yet in a negative sentence → present perfect
how long + an unfinished action → present perfect continuous

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

items.sentence: Nadia ___ (write) two chapters of her story so far.
We ___ (rehearse) since four o'clock, and we're exhausted.
I ___ (not/decide) which university to apply to yet.
Mateo ___ (already/pack) his bag, but Sofia hasn't started.
Look at your hands — you ___ (paint) again, haven't you?
This is the longest essay I ___ (ever/write) for this class.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: Sofia started learning the violin four years ago and she still plays it.
It is Liam's first visit to a football stadium.
Nadia began writing her story this morning and she is still writing it now.
We haven't picked a topic for the project so far.
This essay is more difficult than any other essay I've written.
Mateo's parents moved to Lima in 2015 and they still live there.

summary: Present perfect simple: a result, a number, a first time — the action itself matters less than what changed.
Present perfect continuous: an activity and its duration, often with visible evidence now.
For + a duration, since + a starting point — both need the present perfect if the time is unfinished.
A finished time word (yesterday, last year, in 2015 without since) always needs the past simple instead.
Just, already, yet, still and how long are the words that usually give the tense away.
